prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B002 prize for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. I hold it on the science, not on the fact that all six of us arrived at it. The arc runs from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, through the truncated active GLP-1 peptide and receptor biology, to drugs whose benefit on glycaemia, body weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes has been confirmed in large independent trials. The mechanism is clear, the discovery is original, and about two decades of replication have settled the interpretation. Each of the three names carries a distinct, documented part of the discovery core: Holst the human physiology and active forms, Drucker the receptor and proglucagon-peptide biology and its translation, Mojsov the identification and synthesis of the active peptide. I do not see a case for a second part. Adding B001 or B035 would require either more than three people or a split that drops a credited discoverer, and neither candidate has a cleaner attribution than B002.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the real weakness, and the round-1 exchange has not reduced it. Priority for the active peptide among Mojsov, the Habener group and Holst is contested, and none of us has checked it against primary records. Habener is outside the credited list. The three-person cap leaves out Knudsen, whose acylation-based half-life extension is what turned the biology into liraglutide and semaglutide. A citation that stays on physiology honours the idea and not the drug, and I accept that this is a choice with a cost. If the primary record showed Mojsov's contribution to be materially weaker than assumed, my third name would need to be reconsidered.

responses.point: Sandberg moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and asks that the record say this is a judgement under the three-person cap and not a finding that Knudsen's contribution is minor.
responses.response: I agree with that record entry and would put it in our own reasoning as well. Moving to the shared trio is a choice for discovery over translation, and the choice has a cost. I do not read the Knudsen question as settled. Half-life extension by fatty-acid acylation is invention in its own right, not routine development. What decides it for me is the framing of the prize: identification of the active peptide is the step the whole programme rests on, and nobody disputes that Knudsen's work came after it. I would also accept your point that a contested priority claim is a reason to examine the record carefully, not to drop a name by default. If the evidence on Mojsov came back weak, I would not defend her slot on principle.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that every alternative has an equal or worse attribution problem, that the B002 dispute concerns one name among well-documented contributors, and that the citation should be narrow enough not to write out Habener and others.
responses.response: I accept both halves. The dispute over Mojsov is about one slot, not about whether the discovery is real, and the alternatives are more exposed: six credited names for optogenetics, and an uncredited Eshhar for CAR-T. I also agree that we cannot fix the omissions by adding names under a cap of three. The only honest remedy is a citation that claims what these three did. I have therefore worded mine around the physiology of GLP-1 and the identification of its active form, and not around the discovery of GLP-1 as a whole. My limit is that narrow wording protects the citation but does not remove the omission of Habener, and the record should say so openly.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, sets out that the open questions are the third name, the citation wording and whether a fallback is viable, and in round 1 ranked optogenetics (Boyden, Nagel, Deisseroth) as the first alternative.
responses.response: On the open questions, my answers are these. The third name stays with Mojsov unless the primary record weakens her claim. If it does, Knudsen takes the slot and the citation must say plainly that the framing has moved from discovery to translation. I would not hide that shift. On fallbacks, I keep CAR-T ahead of optogenetics, which I know is the reverse of your order. My reason is not that a tool is lesser than a therapy. It is that I cannot yet name three optogenetics laureates without serious injustice to Hegemann, Bamberg, Miesenböck or Boyden, while the CAR-T difficulty is narrower and can be addressed in the wording. I declared my neuroscience background in round 1, and it pushes me to discount optogenetics, not favour it.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius says the Eshhar omission could make any June, Sadelain and Rosenberg trio unfair, and that she is unsure a second part for engineered T cells is warranted or that GLP-1 should be accompanied by it.
responses.response: I agree that the Eshhar omission and Rosenberg's different role are real obstacles, and they are why I keep B035 as a fallback and not a second part. Rosenberg's adoptive transfer and early gene-modified T-cell work is related to CAR design but is a separate step. A trio of June, Sadelain and Rosenberg would need a citation that fits all three and still leaves Eshhar unexplained. I would accept B035 only if the committee settled that framing first. Your uncertainty about a second part is also mine. With a three-person cap, a second part could only be added by thinning B002, and I do not want to do that.

responses.point: Linnarsson would reconsider the third name if the Mojsov evidence proved weak, and treats B001 as the strong second choice while saying he is less comfortable with it as a prize because of its six credible names.
responses.response: I share your conditional on Mojsov and your discomfort with the six-name problem in B001. Where I differ is only the order of the fallbacks. You place optogenetics second on impact in experimental neuroscience, which I do not dispute. For a Medicine prize I weigh the disease-level or clinical consequence more heavily, and CAR-T has approved products and long follow-up. I recognise that this is a weighting judgement and that CAR-T has its own credit problem. We agree that neither fallback is cleaner than B002, so I do not think the difference between us affects the preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the primary record supports Mojsov's priority for identifying and characterising the active truncated GLP-1 peptide against the Habener group and Holst. I have not verified this and the secretariat check requested by the chair is still the key missing evidence.

Whether excluding Knudsen is defensible if the committee wants the prize to recognise the therapy as well as the discovery, and whether the citation can state this as a judgement without implicitly writing out Habener.

Which fallback to prefer, B035 or B001, if B002 stalls on credit; the choice depends on how a therapy is weighed against a tool and on how Eshhar and Rosenberg, or the six optogenetics names, can be handled.
Long-term safety and durability of weight loss under incretin therapy are still being characterised, though I do not think this undercuts the core discovery.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I have a 2019 co-authored review with Sten Grillner and a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann; neither is a credited name on any shortlisted ballot and I do not request recusal. I note Perlmann's disclosed co-authorship with me. My work in motor-circuit neuroscience touches B001 only as a method; I have tried to apply the common criteria and not give my own field credit for familiarity. I have no documented involvement with B002, B035 or B001.
